title: Why Ribera del Duero tastes the way it does

lede.text: Ribera del Duero is high, dry and cold at night, with days and nights 15 to 20ºC apart while the grapes ripen. That slow ripening builds deep colour and sweetens the tannin on its own.

chapters.title: A river and a high plateau
paras: The vineyards sit on the northern Castilian meseta, the great plateau of the Iberian Peninsula. The Duero runs through them and links more than 100 villages in a belt about 115 km long and 35 km wide. Four provinces meet here: Burgos, Segovia, Soria and Valladolid.
The valleys average between 750 and 850 m above sea level. The hills between the rivers rise to 1,014 m. This height strongly shapes the climate.

fly.label: The Duero belt
fly.caption: The Duero ties together more than 100 villages along a vine belt about 115 km long and 35 km wide.

fly.label: Pintia, where wine was drunk in the 4th century BC
fly.caption: Vessels from the Vaccaean-Roman site of Pintia show wine was served and drunk here as early as the 4th century BC.

chapters.title: Hot days, freezing nights
paras: The climate is Mediterranean, with a strongly continental character and some Atlantic influence. The yearly swing is extreme: 42ºC at the highest and -20ºC at the lowest. Frost can threaten the vines from 17 September to 6 June, and it has hit them many times during the growing cycle.

Rain is moderate to low and summers are dry. Aranda de Duero averages 435 mm, and rainfall rises from west to east. In summer the vines need more water than falls, so the soil has to act as the moisture store.

The sun shines for more than 2,400 hours a year. At ripening the days are warm and the nights cold, with differences of 15 to 20ºC. By day the grapes build the compounds that matter. At night the cold stops the vine from burning them off. The ripening is long and slow, and that sweetens the tannin naturally.

chapters.title: Sandy clay and river terraces
paras: The river basin formed in the Miocene and is filled with sediment. Layers of silty or clayey sand alternate with limestone and marl. The usual soils are ochre and red sandy clays from the Tertiary, and the middle and lower terraces of the Duero.
These soils are basic in pH and short of organic matter.

chapters.title: Tinto Fino, kept in check
paras: Tempranillo is the main red grape, and the locals call it Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. Reds must be at least 75% Tempranillo. It behaves differently here than elsewhere, which is why it has so many local names.
The result is balanced natural acidity, deep colour with blue tones that last, and tannin of high quality. Most of the wines are aged, and the aged reds are among the longest-lived in Spain.

The land is borderline, so the grower has to hold back. The load on the vines must stay low and late varieties are out. Yields are capped at 7,000 kg of grapes per hectare. Historic average yields sit only slightly above half of that cap.
Whites are built on Albillo Mayor, called Blanca del País locally, with at least 75% in the blend. Its cap is 9,500 kg per hectare. In small amounts it also goes into reds to add freshness.

terms.text: The wine spends at least 3 months in oak barrels of up to 600 litres, whether or not it fermented there.
Reds age 24 months, with at least 12 in oak. Rosés and whites age 18 months, with at least 6 in oak.
Reds age 36 months, with at least 12 in oak and the rest in bottle. Rosés and whites age 24 months, with at least 6 in oak.
Reds age 60 months, with at least 24 in oak and the rest in bottle. Rosés and whites age 48 months, with at least 6 in oak.
